player.name: Brakka Stonejaw
player.concept: a loud half-orc barbarian with a big axe, a short temper and a secret love of poetry

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Late-afternoon light slants across the crossroads, catching on a weathered milestone and an empty gibbet. A dead ox lies in the ditch, crude arrows jutting from its flank. Crows watch from the blackthorn hedges, where the wind carries a faint smell of woodsmoke.

A mud-caked farmer jabs his pitchfork at the hedge, then shouts at the milestone as if it has answered him. His eyes are bloodshot; his hands shake with exhaustion. Suddenly, he spots you and swings the pitchfork your way. “You—! Stand there! Are you goblins in disguise?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I throw my arms wide and bellow with laughter. "GOBLINS? Do goblins stand seven feet tall and smell this magnificent, little man?" I squint at the milestone. "And what has the stone been saying to you? Did it insult your mother? Point me at it. I will split it in two."

transcript.speaker: tam
transcript.text: *Tam’s pitchfork wavers between Brakka and the milestone. A frightened laugh cracks out of him.* “Don’t you go splitting stones, turnips save us! It ain’t the stone—well, it didn’t say anything. I was shouting at the hedge. There’s little green devils in there, and they killed my ox!” *He jabs the pitchfork at the arrows, then lowers it a fraction.* “You’re… not a goblin, then? You look awful big to be one.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I lean down close to Tam, conspiratorial. "Not a goblin. But I will tell you a secret, farmer: I was raised by goblins. Three winters in a warren under the Blackmoor hills. I speak their tongue like a native." I cup my hands around my tusks and roar at the hedge in a guttural goblin snarl: "OI! SNOTLINGS! COME OUT AND PARLEY! BRAKKA BRINGS CHEESE!"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Your goblin roar rolls down the drovers’ track. For a heartbeat, the hedges give nothing back—then Tam’s pitchfork dips, and he catches your arm as if you’re the first solid thing he’s seen all day.

He spills it in a breathless rush: the ox, the little green devils in the hedges, the toll-house men laughing him away. As he speaks, his free hand keeps drifting to a lump beneath his smock. The crows shift on the gibbet, watching.

transcript.speaker: tam
transcript.text: *Tam grips your arm tighter, then notices and lets go, wiping his palm on his muddy coat.* “You really know their tongue? Saints bless you—then they heard you. They’ve been following me since dawn, ever since they killed my ox on the drovers’ track. Toll-house fools said I’d been at the cider.” *He glances toward the hedge, then down the road.* “Walk me home to Hollis Farm? Bet’s there, an hour down the track. I—I can’t have the little devils follow me to her door.”
